titleStmt.title: Interview with David C. Speicher, Undated
titleStmt.author: Thomas J. Healy II

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with David C. Speicher was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- me, asking you the questions.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So you've got to -- when I ask you where -- you know, where were you born, or when were you born, and where did you grow up and -- and -- and that, you're going to say, "I was born" -- bup, bup. "I was raised" -- bup, bup. "I went to" -- you know. "My mom" -- Is that you or me? That's my other one. Hold on a second.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Just trying to throw this thing out the window.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: No. We shipped a lot of things that we had that we couldn't do. We dealt with American Optical, Bausch and Lomb, and there was another one. There was three companies in Wilmington that we -- we shipped to. But we got blanks, and I cut and edged them right there at the lab. Well, we had our own place right there in Georgetown. And those stones that cuts -- that cuts these glasses are so fine, you could lay your finger on there, and it don't even cut the hide. That's how fine it is. You would -- if you talk about -- you talk about putting a edge on a knife, I used to take my pocketknife, and I'd take the side of the stone. You can't use the face of the stone, because if you do, the grease in your finger will put oil on that stone, and it will make that -- it will chip that lens when you edge it. So yeah. That's -- In fact, I said something to Dr. Halpern's place at -- here down at Rehoboth. We was in there, and she said -- said, "Are you" --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Here's some water for you right here if you need it.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: I won't need it.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Before we start --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: The more I drink, the more I go to the bathroom.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: [inaudible]

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: But anyhow --

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Yes. Yes. Good.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Um --

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Uh, yeah. Okay. Very good. I'm at work. My wife might be able to come tomorrow morning. Excellent. Thank you so much. Yeah. Bye-bye. Thanks.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. So the first thing we're going to do is you're going to give me your -- your full --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Age, rank and serial number.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No, no. Just your -- your full name and then spell your last name.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: S-P-E-I-C-H-E-R.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: It's German.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: What's your name?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: German -- Speicher. German.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Were you here early?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You weren't supposed to be here at 2:30?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Yeah. And the -- this woman called this morning. I didn't think -- she was supposed to call last night, and I didn't think I was coming down. She called -- so I went someplace else this morning. She called --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Who called?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Some --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Allison?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Allison?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Some woman called my wife and said --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Allison maybe?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: -- down at 1:00. So anyhow --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, at 1.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: So anyhow --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I wonder what -- Baker -- Ralph Baker was. Okay. Good. I'm glad you said that because I was expecting Ralph.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Ralph Baker?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: From Bridgeville?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: I know Ralph Baker, but he ain't from Bridgeville. He's dead.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Well, maybe he didn't -- did he just die?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: No. He's -- he's older than I am.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Somebody else. I don't know.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Yeah. I was telling you when I went to the senior thing down in Rehoboth --

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: -- Halpern, I was in there talking to Halpern, telling him. She said, "Would you be interested in going back to work again?" I said, "Well, I hadn't given it much thought, but I might." Apparently they have trouble getting people that know what to do. Because we --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Ralph -- no. Ralph -- Ralph lives in Laurel.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: No. That's another Ralph.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You're in Bridgeville?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Yeah. The Ralph Baker I knew has been dead for a good while.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I was at a parade in Bridgeville, many years ago.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Fireman's parade.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: The convention was there one year.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Right. You're right.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I was a very young --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: I was a fire -- I was a fire police.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I was a very young child, and I think I had -- might have had my first beer on the road in those days.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Uh-huh. They had a big --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Is there a Town Court Hot -- Motel there or something? Not a Town Court?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Yeah. It was a motel out on the road.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Ran by Mr. and Mrs. Walter Betts.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I think I still have -- I think that was probably '62 --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Way back. Yeah.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: That's when the building -- then the building they're now in was first built.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: There was actually a guy that worked at the post office there, too, who was a surfer.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Well, I don't know about that. I worked at the post office.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: He was -- what was that guy's name? He served over at Ocean City, Maryland.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Oh, Harzday [phonetic]?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, God. He sold surfboards, too.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: I don't know. Bob Bennett -- Bob Bennett was there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: It might have been Bob Bennett. He would be --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Bob Bennett was the postmaster. He left Bridgeville and went to --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No, no, no, no. This would have been a guy -- I'm --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Carney? How about a Carney? Carney was a captain -- a fisherman. He was captain out of Ocean City.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: He also went to the beach a lot. I don't know what he done.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, let's see. This guy was -- this guy was -- I would have been 15. He might have been 20 at the time. So he'd be about 65 right now maybe.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Yeah. It might be -- it might have been that Carney boy. Rick --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: It might have been.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: -- Rick Carney.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I thought it was Bill something or other. Anyway --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: No. That's --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: All right. So anyways, give me your -- give me your full name, and then spell your last name. Let's do that again.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: David C. Speicher, S-P-E-I-C-H-E-R.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. And what you can do is just tell me a little story about the whole thing, but I'm going to -- when were you born, where did you grow up, who your parents were and what they did, and then did you have any brothers and sisters.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So go ahead.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: I was born in Greenwood, Delaware, June the 14th, 1923. We lived on a farm. Graduated from Greenwood High School in 1941. Had two sisters and four brothers, and three of the four of us were in the service. Two of our brothers died -- two of my brothers, Robert and Randall, died, both with service-connected disabilities. Robert was in World War II in the Solomon Islands, and Randall was in during the Korean War as a male nurse in Germany. And Howard stayed home on the farm and grew crops and vegetables so that we would have something to eat. And two sisters grew up in Greenwood and graduated from Greenwood. Both of -- well, one of them has passed away. They worked in -- one of them worked in a hosiery mill, and -- well, both of them worked in the hosiery mill for a while. And then the elder one -- the oldest one did. And she got married and went to Claymont. Her husband worked in the shipyard during the war, World War II. And the youngest sister was a nurse. And her husband was a captain, was a doctor, a medical doctor, in the Philippines during World War II.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Which -- which sister had the husband that was in the shipyard?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Iva.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Is she -- is he still alive?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: They are both -- they -- she has passed away, and so has her husband.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. Now, your mom and -- what's your -- what was your dad's name?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: My dad's name was Harry Earl Speicher. He moved down here from the cove in Maryland. Accident, Maryland. And Mother's name was Martha Emma.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And your dad was a farm -- had a farm?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Had a farm. We started with a small 50-foot-long chicken house, and we -- every time we made enough money, Dad would build 50 more feet on till we got up to where it was 275 feet long. And we grew chickens. And when the war broke out, I had deferments for once or twice, and then it was either I or my other brother Howard that was going to go in service. So he was married and had a child and expecting another one. So I told Dad, "They're going to get me after a while anyhow. You'd better put him on the farm and I'll go." So I went to -- that's when I went in service.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How big a farm was -- how big of acreage was it?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: It was 90-acre farm with 45 acres clear.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Still have it?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: No. It's been sold.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How many chickens did you have?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: 7500. We got it -- we started with 1500 and got it up to 7500. And that's when we -- that's when the chicken business first started back in 1939.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: And we grew chickens and then grew other crops, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How come it's so -- how come there's -- how come chicken prices have gone up just recently?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Because of the cost of production, the cost of labor. Now -- most of our feed then consisted of corn and soybeans, which was grown around here. Now there's a lot of chemicals that has to go in the chicken feed. My wife worked in research with chickens for 25 years. And a lot of this yellow that you see in the chicken is in there from a chemical.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Can you hear her?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Is she saying something?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. So tell me -- tell me when you went in the service, how you went in -- you know, how you went in, when you -- you know, when you -- oh, here's -- here's -- first, before we get to that -- and I want you to repeat the December 7. December 7, 1941, do you remember it and when and --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- where and -- And where were you? So repeat --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: I was sitting in my uncle's dining room, and my two cousins and a neighbor boy were all four sitting around a table playing cards when the bombing took place, and we heard it on the radio on December the 7th, 1942.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: One.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: One.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. So tell me -- so say -- say again --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- December 7, 1941.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: That's where we were sitting.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No. Say that.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: December 7, 1941. We were sitting around the table playing cards, two cousins and a neighbor's boy, at my uncle's house.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And what did you think about that? What did -- what -- did that mean anything to you then or --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: No. Not -- not too much because then, I was only about -- oh, boy, I just got out of school. And at that time, I was working for a chicken man, was catching chickens and hauling live chickens. And we just figured we'd be going to work the next day. Monday morning, we did. And then I went home on the farm and started expanding with the chickens and farming and hauling chickens to the city and continued on. And then they started to draft. So I knew that sooner or later, that they would draft me anyhow. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So then you got your -- go ahead. Tell me -- tell me about when you went in -- when you -- where you went to get drafted and where your induction was and then you went to boot camp and --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Oh, okay. We signed up in -- I want to say Seaford, I think. I'm not sure. But anyhow, when I was -- when I went in, I had to go down to Seaford and get a train, and we -- they took us to Fort Dix. And that was in August of 1944. And I went -- I stayed five days at Fort Dix. And we was in there with a whole bunch of other guys, and nobody knew what the other guy done. Everybody was at equal -- equal basis. You all had the same uniform. There was no 100 dollar shoes or 20 dollar ties. You each one had the same fatigues, and the shirts and the pants and everything was alike. And whether you was a millionaire or a pauper on the street, you was all equal basis. And you might have to be on KP the next morning. And one of the boys was called up, and he didn't even know where the kitchen was to be on KP, he was so new at Fort Dix. So we was all a bunch of greenhorns. We went from Fort Dix to Fort Belvoir. And at Fort Belvoir, we was in the engineers, and that's when we took our basic training. And they taught us how to read maps, read a compass and take out on night projects and where to -- they'd take you right out in the middle of the woods and turn you loose with a compass, and you had to be able to read it and get back to certain spots at a certain time. And unfortunately, another fellow and I -- you worked in pairs, two of you at a time. Each worked with another one. You had a buddy system. And we got lost at a swamp. Found a road, and I knew the road went back to Fort Belvoir. I said, "Forget this swamp. I'm getting out of here." We went right back to camp and took a shower and went to bed. The rest of them come in -- I don't know when. But anyhow, when we finished our basic there, we would -- we would go on a march. And sometimes you'd just regular march. It was -- you'd go on a route march. And it would be 3 miles an hour. But if you went on a forced march, you made 10 miles an hour, which meant you would jog for 10 minutes and walk 5. Then you would jog for 10 more minutes and walk 5. And we had a tough drill sergeant. He said, "If you're going to pass out, I want you to pass out right in the middle of the road. If you have to walk over to the ditch, you can make two more steps." And that's what he meant.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How long were you in there?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: I was in there eight weeks. And then I went in what they call the combat engineers, which was an advanced course with heavy equipment. And that's where they taught us how to use demolitions, how to set up bombs, how to set -- run bulldozers, heavy equipment. In fact, they took us to Quantico, and we built a road right through the Quantico Marine base, right through the woods with D8 bulldozers and graders and heavy equipment and pans. And you name it; we had it. And we also went out with demolition. They showed us how to take a -- shoot a bazooka. I qualified for 30-millimeter machine gun, 50-millimeter machine gun. Also the bazooka, which shot a shell that would pierce a one-inch armored tank. And again, you worked the buddy system. And when you -- when you was shooting a bazooka, you got -- your buddy would load it and stand off to one side because the back blast was dangerous within 20 feet of the back of it. So he stood off to the side and tapped you on the head when you had it loaded. And then we shot the tank and ducked in a ditch because you didn't know what -- where that shrapnel was going to go when it hit that tank. And I still have one of the duds home that we used. Some way, I managed to get it out of there. But anyhow, I kept it. It's -- the head was never loaded, but it was a -- if the head had been loaded, it would have pierced a one-inch armored tank. And also we used it -- that's when we used to use the hand grenades. We shot -- we throwed the hand grenades, and they would -- each one of those little squares on a hand grenade, when it goes off, becomes a flying piece of shrapnel. So when you drop them in a tank, nobody comes out alive. That shrapnel cuts them all to pieces because it cut the leaves right off the trees where we was throwing them. And we also was taught how to set demolitions, set bombs, take a handmade -- take a bottle or a can and load it with stones, nails, pieces of metal, whatever you could find to load it, and then stick a charge in there and load dynamite in there and put a cap in it and wrap it around demolition coils of wire and set it off with a match and throw it. And then you run as hard as you could. And that's when we learned to dismantle them. They also taught us how to dismantle landmines. They'd take us out into a minefield, and we'd crawl up on our bellies. You never knew where the landmines were. And all we had to dismantle that landmine with was a bayonet. And they didn't have the charges in them, but they had the caps in them, which would scare you to death when it went off and cover you with mud. And we went through an infiltration course with a 70-pound pack, and the sergeant told us, he said -- they were shooting over top of us at 30 feet high -- 30 inches, so at 30 inches high. And he said, "If you don't think those bullets are live, look in the back of you at that bank where those bullets are hitting and watch the stones fly." And of course some of them raised up with their buttocks a little too high, and you know what happened with that -- with that 30 inches. So then later on, I found out that they raised it to 36. But we went through there, and it was -- it was a minefield. And you went through mud, water, whatever, because if you deviated from your line of travel, chances are you would hit a landmine, and it would go off. So you had to go right through -- if water laid in the path where you was going, you went right on through it, mud, water and all. And when we went there -- then we left there and went to Fort Myer. And that's when we took the military police training. And we were in the old guard -- what they call now the old guard at the Fort Myer in Arlington, Virginia. And that's where I spent the rest of my time. Most of it was spent right there doing police work. Our battalion was the 730 MP battalion, which was a security battalion for the capital of the United States, Washington, DC. And twice, we had to lock the city down and close everything off to secure it for -- for security reasons. One time was when they had the end of the war in Europe. And the next time was when the war ended in Japan. Twice, we -- our -- we were scheduled to ship out two different times in the engineers with the heavy equipment to go to the Solomon Islands. I missed that by two days. Our whole -- our whole company was going. And we missed that by two days. And the next time we were scheduled to go was at Fort Myer for police work in Japan. And we had our flu shots and ev -- all kinds of shots that you needed, tetanus, whatever, to go into Japan and do the police work in Japan. And we was fortunate again. Missed that by one day. Twenty-four hours and they cancelled the orders. And somebody wanted to know what I was doing during that 24 hours. And I told them, "Praying." I didn't want any parts of that police work in Japan. Not after World War II.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How long after that did you get out?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Got out in June of '46. And -- but while we was at Fort Myer, one of the main things that I remember distinctly was we was there during the time that President Roosevelt passed away. And our whole unit marched in President Roosevelt's funeral parade. And we stood at parade rest for an hour on Constitution Avenue, waiting for the body to come out of the rotunda to go down to Constitution Avenue into Union Station to be shipped to New York. And of course, we was confined to barracks for three days during that time, as we were setting it up so that Truman could be sworn in as next President of the United States. And we couldn't even go to the PX. We couldn't go anywhere except stay in the barracks for three days. And it took three days to do it. And when Truman was sworn in, I was on the north gate of the White House with a .45 caliber semiautomatic pistol loaded. And nobody went through the gate. DOD said, "Nobody will go through the gate." I said, "Sir, the gate is locked." He said, "Nobody goes through the gate." And it was on the north gate of the White House. And that yard -- that's -- is big. That's why it's so large, that helicopters can go in and out of the north yard of the White House. It's that big.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So then you came back and came back here?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And you started back working on the farm?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: No. I came back here and went to work for a construction outfit that summer. And then after that summer, I went to work for a grocery company, delivering groceries. For a year and a half, I done -- about a year and a half, I done that on the groceries. And then I had a chance to go into automotive parts department, working for Conway Motors which is on the circle in Georgetown. At that time, they had there. And then also was also a serviceman for Maytag washers. And they came out, and I was sent away to school for that and done service work on the Maytags and also worked in the parts department as assistant shop foreman for Mr. Conway. And then I went into optician for Dr. West and took two years of that. And from there, I went to Dover as a legislator. I was elected in 1952 on paper ballots. And we counted ballots till, like -- oh, I guess maybe 3 or 4:00 in the morning. And I thought, you know, there's got to be a better way than sitting up till 3 or 4:00 in the morning counting paper ballots. And I made up my mind, if I was fortunate enough to get to Dover and could, then I would try to see if we couldn't get a better way. And we did, because they came in with a voting machine. And in nineteen fifty -- my term was 1953 and '54. And in 1953, they came up with a voting machine, put it in the state house and legislative hall, and demonstrated it, and brought a miniature machine in to show us what it was. And the very first thing I did was went up and talked to the governor, who then was Caleb Boggs. And I said, "If I'm fortunate enough, Governor, to get this bill passed through the house chamber and the senate chamber, will you sign the bill?" And he said yes. And we were setting there with a one majority in the house, which meant everybody in the majority was a king. It took everybody's vote to pass the bill. And I thought this is a good time. I'm going to get this bill introduced on the floor. And I did. And I got a friend of mine from -- Glenn Lowe, who was from Laurel, to work the opposite side, which was the Democrat side. I was a Republican at that time. And I got Glenn Lowe, who's a Democrat, on his side to see how many votes he could get to help with the bill. And when we called the bill up on the floor, we had ten cosponsors on the bill. And it went through the house just like it had roller skates.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Were you -- were you in the house or senate?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: House.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: House.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: House chamber.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How long did you st -- were you there?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: One term. Then they rotated. Everybody -- in all the election districts, they rotated. Nobody succeeded themselves, because the governor called me up and wanted to know if I would be interested in running for the senate because Mr. Walter Hoy, who was a good friend of mine, was a Democrat on the other side, was going to run for senator. And they was going to run me against Walter Hoy. And I said, "No. I'm -- I'm not going to run against Mr. Hoy." I called him "Doc Hoy." And I said, "No. I am not running against Doc Hoy because Doc Hoy helped me get several bills passed." And another bill that got passed was putting the state police on a 40-hour week. At that time, the state police, when they bought a -- wrote a ticket, they had to appear in court. They had to go on their own time, which wasn't quite fair with the boys on the road. They might sit in the judge's office for an hour or two with no money. They'd go to court and sit there and wait. So we got a 40-hour week for the state police at that time, too. And they got those two bills, main bills. There were several others that went through. But anyhow, the bill went to the house chamber. And when it got to the senate, I thought now they might just pigeonhole this bill over here. And I went to find out what committee the bill was in. And when I found out what the committee was, I went to the chairman of the committee, and I told him -- it goes back to playing the old game of trading horses. And I told him, I said, "If you expect to get any bills of yours passed through the house, we want this bill out of your committee and on the floor and through the senate as quick as possible because the governor's waiting for it." And he brought it out. It passed the senate. The governor signed it. And we had the first voting machines in the state of Delaware. And I have today the first miniature voting machine in my house, that ever came in Delaware. The ?chute? company gave it to me as a gift. So now then, they've brought it up -- I mean, now they have the electronic machines, but when they first came out, you had the big lever that you pulled and all of the candidates on that ballot was voted for at one shot.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Now they're in -- now, each one, you vote independent.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What -- what major message would you leave for generations to come about the war, about the -- just --

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Well, I would -- I would say that a lot of us gave a lot of sacrifices. When we was in service -- just to give you an example how everybody was put on an equal basis. Incidentally, our salary when we was in service, drafted, was 50 dollars a month. And that's all we got. And one of the fellows that we was in there with, when I was stationed in Fort Myer -- just to show you that they didn't pick and choose, he was a tailor in civilian life for the movie stars in California. And he tailored -- tailored our uniforms to fit. Our shirts were tailor fitted. And he had a tailor shop up in the attic of our barracks, where he tailored all the -- all the boys' uniforms. And he also put a beading on their overseas cap and fixed them up nice. So when we went out on the parade field, we was the best-looking company there was on the field, and there was four companies of us. And one of the fellows that was in -- another fellow was in there was a part owner in King's Ranch in Texas. So it didn't make any difference what you were. You were all on equal basis, and you done the same thing. And we -- there was -- there was a lot of guys -- this guy that was from King Ranch, they broke -- when they broke through the Battle of the Bulge, he was in a foxhole. And they said all night long, the Germans run over that foxhole that he was hiding in. And he stayed there until they pushed them back the next day, the next afternoon. Now, can you imagine him living in that foxhole with, you know -- anytime they would have caught him, it would have been sure death. They would have shot him right there. And he knew it. And a lot of these guys come back -- I saw guys come back that was a nervous wreck that they'd wake up at night, and you know, and we'd go help what we could and do what we could. Different things that you did. And you just done -- you done your job, whatever it was. Part of the -- part of our security also got the people that worked in the Pentagon building. That came under our jurisdiction. And we had to move that traffic in and out of that Pentagon building every night and every morning. And they had 35,000 people working in there. And when you're moving traffic, nobody stops. You move -- you move them. They gave us 30 minutes to empty a parking lot. And you bet one thing -- we criticize a lot of these people in Washington, DC, because the minute that light turns green, they're gone. And that's why. Because if they don't, they've got so much traffic over in Washington, DC, that you -- if you stop traffic for a minute, you've got traffic backed up for 2 miles. And they'll hook a wrecker on you in a heartbeat and tow you right out in the middle of a field. They don't care. They want that traffic moving. And they don't care who you are. The colonel told us, he said, "Tag anybody that's up to a colonel." He said, "But if he's over a colonel, boys," he said, "I can't take him. He outranks me." He said, "Leave the stars alone." He said, "I can't -- I can't do nothing with him." But we could -- we could tag anything up to a full colonel. And they got them out of there. And they moved them. And I would just -- I'd -- I'd say that anybody -- all these young children, if -- when they got out of school, probably a good thing for them would be to serve maybe a year, for disciplinary problems, if nothing else. It would teach you how to live on your own. And it would teach you security. It would teach them how to take orders, how to take commands, how to respond, how to respond quickly. And you have to think for yourself because when you're there, there's nobody there but you. And you've got to come up with the right answer. If you don't, then guess what? If you're overseas someplace and somebody's got their eyesights trained on you, and you make a mistake, you ain't going to get the second chance. I know in dem -- when I first got out of service, I done a lot of dynamiting for farmers with ditches and stumps and things like that. I had several people that asked me, you know, "What happens if you make a mistake?" I said, "Sir, you don't get but one chance. And if you make a mistake, it will be your last one." When you've got a pocket full of dynamite sticks and -- and it's about 25 in each pocket, there ain't going to be too much left of you. The undertaker won't have enough to put in a rubber bag. So you -- you've got -- you've got to be right. And it learns you to be accurate and responsive. I think this ROTC program that they have in schools is a very good thing to -- to show. I see it in Woodbridge. I live right next to the school. And I see those -- those students that are taking ROTC. They -- when they come down the alley in a jog, I speak to them or say something. They don't even notice you're there, and they're not supposed to. They got their mind on one thing, and that's their job and their job only. And that's what they're supposed to do. And some of them are very good at it. And they present the colors. And I've noticed -- having -- having worked over in Washington where the colors are presented, having worked -- And incidentally, we also had to be able to walk the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, which is a very, very, very discreet group. And they don't make mistakes, and they can't. And they get -- they only work one hour on and three hours off. That's all they could stand. And they only -- and they only pull 10 years of that duty. And then they're out of there. And -- and we had -- our unit had to be able to do that. So it was a lot of things that we had to do and had to learn to do and had to cope with. And I remember one time, they sent us out on a line shack for guard duty. There was nothing out there but this building and cots. And we slept in our clothes for a week. They gave us a can of C rations, which is about as big as a sardine can, and a quart of water. Once a day, that truck would come in and drop everybody off. They'd fill their canteen with a quart of water and a can of sar -- of C rations. That's as big as a sardine can, and that's -- that's what we had to eat and live on till the truck came in the next day. And we done that for a week.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: See, and you only had to do it for a day.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: But what they're teaching you is survival.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: See, being an old farm boy, I had learned on the farm that you had to take -- when you went down to the lower field to work on the farm, you took a jug of water with you, and it had to last you till dinnertime, so you didn't drink it all one time. And I learned right quick on that quart of water to kind of sip on it all day long. Now, one of these other city boys was along there, and he took his right on down. By 10:00, he was out. By 2:00, he wanted a drink of my water. I said, "No. I don't think so." I said, "Tomorrow when it comes in, you learn to sip your water, and you learn to make it last all day long." And we also went through bayonet practice. We also went through certain things in judo. We learned the three strategic points that it takes to kill a man. This was all part of a police training.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I'm surprised you didn't come back here and become, like, chief of Bridge -- Bridgeville.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: When we got ready to be discharged, the captain of the metropolitan police department came out and interviewed every company. And there was four companies of us. He interviewed every company, one at a time, and offered us a job with the metropolitan police at the same rank that we held in the service, and I was a sergeant. And he said, "The minute you get your discharge at Fort Meade," he said, "you come right back to Washington, DC." And he said, "We'll put you right on the payroll, and you have a job." And at that time, I had had about two years. I'd had enough of police work, and I didn't want anything to do with any more people in Washington, DC.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: It was -- it had got to the point where it just -- you just couldn't -- Well, when we'd have a parade or something like that, we'd have to -- we'd have to direct the traffic, and we'd have to -- like, we had a war bond drive. And we were standing at the gate to get into that entertainment; had movie stars and everything else in there. Sergeant Gaither and I were on the gate. And to get in that gate, you had to have a 50 dollar war bond, where you had bought one. We had over 200,000 people that were seated. And it was that many standing around outside at the Washington Monument. They was from the Washington Monument, clear down to Constitution Avenue. And I forget how many movie stars were down there. General Wainwright was there. He'd come back from overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Is that at the end?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: That was at the end.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Because he was a prisoner, right, for a long time?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Yeah. That was when he came back, and they had a big par --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: -- parade at Washington, DC. And we was on that gate. And my wife was within 50 feet of me and couldn't find me. There was that many people. And the only way she found me was I had to go to the bathroom, and I went down to the barracks -- the WAVE barracks was right there close. And I went down there to their latrine. And she saw me go by and called me. And her and my brother were standing there. He was in the Navy. He had just got back from overseas. And she called me, and I got them and walked them underneath the wire and set them down and said, "I'll be back." And I came back and stood and we went on back.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- you okay?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: I screwed up anything?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: That was easy, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: It wasn't bad. Yeah. Are you all done?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: I have to also -- you didn't know I also was up to Dover when Brad Barnes was speaker. I was sergeant at arms for five years on the main door.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, you were?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: He found out some way -- because we was security, and he found out some way through the police department what I had done at Washington, DC. And he said, "I want you on that main door when I'm speaker to serve because I want somebody there that knows protocol." And I knew it. When you have a joint session, you have to use regular protocol or you go through. Like you introduce your --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: -- county officials, your state officials. And you -- there's a certain order that you go through. And the last one you go through as senators come in. And the last one you go through is the governor and his entourage. And they have to be introduced and escorted by people in the house chamber to the podium for him to address --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: -- him or her, whichever it may be, to address the joint session.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So what do you think of Carney being lieutenant governor?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: I have no -- I have no quarrels with Carney being the -- as far as I'm concerned -- I told him -- he was sitting up there one day. We was up there some time ago for some historical thing, I forget what it was now, but anyhow, each farmer -- legislator was invited. And we went up there, and it was held in joint session. It was held in the senate chamber.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: And so we stayed -- after everything was over, we went back and went into senate, sit there. We went in the house. And of course they introduced us and -- wife and I. And then we went in the senate and sat over there for a while. And he runs a tight ship. And I told him. I said, "I'll be very frank with you." I said, "They don't get away with too much over here. You keep things in line."

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Has the Republican candidate been down here?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Bruce Marshall, has he been down?

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. We've met him. Yeah. Yeah. Either one of them would be good. And I've told several people, "Whether Carney gets it or whether Usher Marshall gets it, I know who the winners are going to be." And they wanted to know who. I said, "The people." Because whichever one gets it, you're going to get a good person in the office, which is what you need. But it's hard to get any -- I've been asked several times to run again, and I've turned it down. I don't want any parts of it because there's so many in there now that they're in there for their own selfish things that they want for their own things. And it's wrong. You're in there to do whatever you do for all those people in the state of Delaware. And I said just because you go in there from Sussex County or Kent County or Newcastle, it doesn't mean that it's -- that those are the only ones you're going to represent. When you represent and you vote on a bill, it affects everybody in the state of Delaware. It don't just affect that person that lives in your district. It affects everybody. And that's what you should be looking at. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. You okay?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: It's hot, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Oh, it's hot.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Anything else you need?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: No air. You've got to have air. Air, we need. Air, air.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: We need fresh air.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Turn that light off. That light's get --

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Not too bad.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: Yeah. I -- if -- I had somebody ask me. They said, "If you're asked to go back as a sergeant at arms, do you think you would go?" I said, "Well, I might probably if I -- if I thought it" -- I'm a DAV, and this leg bothers me some. And if I could -- if I thought I could do it, I probably would. Because you need somebody. And I've watched -- with no disrespect to anybody, I've watched -- Leave the door. It don't bother me.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: It's warm in here.

sp.speaker: David C. Speicher
sp.p: But I've watched them work -- (Conclusion of interview.)
